chunks: Driving a motor in both directions. The question: What if you need to drive the motor in both directions?
To run a DC motor both ways, you must reverse the current through it. The standard circuit is an H-bridge: four switches arranged around the motor like the letter H.
Closing one diagonal pair sends current one way through the motor. The other pair sends it back. A PWM signal on one switch sets the speed.
The one forbidden state is turning on both switches on the same side.
Imagine a toy car with a battery you can flip by hand. One way it goes forward. Flipped, it reverses.
An H-bridge flips the battery electronically, using four switches, two at a time.
The danger is like shorting the battery with a wire: if the top and bottom switch on one side close at once, they short the supply.
Forward: Q₁ and Q₄ on. Current runs from V M through Q₁, left to right through the motor, and down through Q₄ to ground. Reverse swaps to Q₃ and Q₂.
The animated wires show where current flows.
H-bridge: four switches in an H shape, with the motor as the crossbar. Shoot-through: both switches on one side (one leg) on at once, shorting the supply.
PWM: switching fully on and off very fast. The fraction of time on (the duty) sets the average voltage.
Dead time: a short gap between one switch turning off and its partner turning on.
Call the switches Q1 and Q2 on the left (top, bottom) and Q3 and Q4 on the right. With 12 volts, Q1 and Q4 on gives forward at +12 volts.
Q3 and Q2 on gives reverse at minus 12 volts. Both low sides on, Q2 and Q4, shorts the motor and brakes it. All off is coast.
Q1 and Q2 together is the forbidden state: with two 10 milliohms switches, the short is 12 over 0. 02 equals 600 amps on paper.
For speed, chop one switch at 50% duty and the motor sees an average of 6 volts. That is the whole idea.
"An H-bridge: four switches around the motor. Turning on the top-left and bottom-right sends current one way; top-right and bottom-left the other way. PWM one switch for speed.
Never turn on both switches of one leg, so I add dead time or use a driver IC with shoot-through protection.
Body diodes carry freewheel current, both low sides give braking, all off is coast. The MCU drives it with PWM plus a direction pin or two inputs."
Quick check. In an H-bridge with switches Q1 (top-left), Q2 (bottom-left), Q3 (top-right), Q4 (bottom-right), which pair drives the motor forward and which the reverse?
